woke_trap_assessment.explanation: NOT A WOKE TRAP. The Electric State does not disguise its ideological leanings behind a traditional marketing campaign. The trailers prominently feature Millie Bobby Brown as a defiant, independent teenage lead navigating a post-apocalyptic landscape with a band of misfit robots. The found-family structure, anti-corporate messaging, and girl-on-a-mission framing are all visible from the marketing. Conservative viewers who dislike these tropes can identify them before watching. The film is exactly what it looks like: a big-budget Netflix spectacle with mildly progressive themes wrapped in a CGI-heavy adventure. No bait-and-switch.

financials.totalViews: 74.2 million views in first half of 2025 (158.2 million hours)
financials.context: One of the most expensive films ever made. Opening week viewership fell below Netflix expectations and trailed behind The Gray Man (also directed by the Russos). Failed to crack Netflix's all-time top 10 films list despite the $320M investment. Netflix's most expensive original film to date.

director.name: Anthony Russo, Joe Russo
director.ideology: CENTER-LEFT CORPORATE PROGRESSIVISM. The Russo Brothers rose to prominence directing Captain America: The Winter Soldier and Civil War, then peaked with Avengers: Infinity War and Endgame, the highest-grossing film of all time. Their post-Marvel work has been defined by massive budgets and diminishing returns: Cherry (2021, 36% RT), The Gray Man (2022, 51% RT), and now The Electric State (14% RT). They have publicly advocated for diversity in Hollywood, supported inclusive casting, and their production company AGBO has positioned itself as a progressive-leaning studio. Their ideological footprint is corporate Hollywood progressive: pro-diversity rhetoric, anti-corporate themes in their films, and a preference for found-family narratives over traditional family structures.
director.profile: Anthony and Joe Russo are American filmmakers who began their careers in television comedy (Arrested Development, Community) before transitioning to Marvel Studios blockbusters. Their MCU run (Captain America: The Winter Soldier, Captain America: Civil War, Avengers: Infinity War, Avengers: Endgame) grossed over $6.8 billion worldwide. Post-Marvel, they signed a massive deal with Netflix and founded AGBO Films. The Electric State represents the most expensive film of their career and arguably their most significant critical failure. The 14% RT score is their lowest ever, falling below even Cherry's 36%. Their screenplay collaborators Christopher Markus and Stephen McFeely co-wrote the script, maintaining the same creative team that produced their MCU work.

writer.name: Christopher Markus, Stephen McFeely
writer.profile: Christopher Markus and Stephen McFeely are the screenwriting duo behind nearly every Russo Brothers film. Their credits include all three Captain America films, Avengers: Infinity War, Avengers: Endgame, and The Gray Man. They also wrote the Chronicles of Narnia trilogy. For The Electric State, they adapted Simon Stalenhag's 2018 illustrated novel, making significant changes to the source material: adding the Chris Pratt character entirely, transforming the tone from melancholic and atmospheric to action-adventure comedy, and restructuring the plot around a corporate villain and climactic battle sequence. Critics widely noted that the adaptation stripped the source material of its haunting, contemplative quality in favor of Marvel-style spectacle.

lead_producer.name: Russell Ackerman, Chris Castaldi, Mike Larocca, Patrick Newall, Anthony Russo, Joe Russo
lead_producer.company: AGBO Films / Double Dream / Skybound Entertainment

composer.name: Alan Silvestri
composer.profile: Alan Silvestri is one of Hollywood's most prolific composers, best known for the Back to the Future trilogy, Forrest Gump, Cast Away, and multiple MCU entries including The Avengers, Infinity War, and Endgame. His score for The Electric State continues his long collaboration with the Russo Brothers. Silvestri's involvement signals the Russos' ambition to replicate their MCU-level production values, though critics noted the score felt generic in the context of the film's derivative storytelling.

fidelityCasting.sourceTitle: The Electric State by Simon Stalenhag (2018)
fidelityCasting.assessment:
The Electric State is adapted from Simon Stalenhag's 2018 illustrated novel of the same name. The source material is a melancholic, atmospheric work set in an alternate 1990s America, following a teenage girl and her robot companion across a decayed technological landscape. The novel is essentially wordless art with sparse narration, closer to a mood piece than a traditional narrative.

The film's casting is largely original since the novel provides minimal character detail. Millie Bobby Brown as Michelle is a reasonable match for the teenage protagonist. Chris Pratt's character Keats does not exist in the source material at all, he was invented entirely for the film adaptation to provide a male lead and comedic foil. This is the most significant departure: the novel is a quiet, solitary journey, while the film transforms it into a buddy-adventure with quippy dialogue.

The voice cast for the robots (Mackie, Harrelson, Cox, Slate, Tudyk, Azaria) represents an entirely original layer. The novel's robots are silent, eerie presences. The film gives them personalities, voices, and comic relief roles. Mr. Peanut, based on the actual Planters mascot, is a film invention.

Stanley Tucci as the corporate villain Ethan Skate is also a film creation. The novel has no central antagonist. The adaptation imposes a conventional hero-vs-corporation structure onto material that was deliberately ambiguous and unresolved.

Ke Huy Quan in a dual role (the human Dr. Amherst and the robot P.C.) is the most interesting casting choice, playing both the conscience of the story and its mechanical echo.

Overall fidelity to source material: LOW. The Russos and Markus/McFeely kept the basic premise (girl and robot cross post-apocalyptic America to find her brother) but rebuilt virtually everything else. The tone, structure, supporting cast, villain, humor, and resolution are all film inventions. Fans of Stalenhag's meditative art book will find almost nothing of its spirit in this $320 million spectacle.

celebrityMentions.name: Millie Bobby Brown
celebrityMentions.context: Stars as Michelle Greene, the teenage protagonist. Brown's performance drew mixed reactions. Supporters note her emotional range in the film's quieter moments, particularly scenes involving her brother. Critics, especially on social media, described her performance as 'monotonic' and compared it unfavorably to her Stranger Things work, arguing she has been typecast as the sassy, bossy young woman in every role since Eleven. The 'Mary Sue' criticism appeared frequently in audience discussions: Michelle is resourceful, brave, defiant toward authority, and ultimately the savior of the story, with minimal vulnerability or failure along the way.

celebrityMentions.name: Chris Pratt
celebrityMentions.context: Plays Keats, a smuggler and war veteran. Pratt's character does not exist in the source novel and was created for the film. His casting represents the Russos' desire to add star power and comedic appeal. Pratt plays essentially the same charming rogue archetype he perfected as Star-Lord in Guardians of the Galaxy. Conservative audiences may appreciate Pratt's presence given his reputation as one of Hollywood's few openly Christian leading men, though his character in this film is a cynical drifter rather than a faith-driven figure.

celebrityMentions.name: Ke Huy Quan
celebrityMentions.context: Plays the dual role of Dr. Clark Amherst (a human scientist) and P.C. (a robot built with Amherst's voice). Quan's Oscar-winning comeback in Everything Everywhere All at Once (2022) made him one of the most celebrated actors in Hollywood. His performance in The Electric State was widely praised as one of the film's highlights, bringing genuine emotion to an otherwise hollow spectacle.

celebrityMentions.name: Stanley Tucci
celebrityMentions.context: Plays Ethan Skate, the CEO of Sentre and the film's primary villain. Skate is a tech mogul who exploited a child's consciousness to build world-dominating technology. The character is a composite of every Silicon Valley villain archetype: polished, smiling, and utterly amoral. Tucci brings his usual sophistication to the role but is given little material beyond standard corporate villainy.

celebrityMentions.name: The Russo Brothers
celebrityMentions.context: Directors Anthony and Joe Russo. The Electric State represents a dramatic fall from their MCU peak. After directing Avengers: Endgame ($2.79 billion worldwide), they signed a massive deal with Netflix. Their first Netflix film, The Gray Man (2022), received mixed reviews. The Electric State, with its $320 million budget and 14% RT score, is being discussed as evidence that the Russos' success was primarily a function of Marvel's IP and Kevin Feige's oversight rather than their own directorial vision. The discourse around the film centers on whether the Russos ever possessed the creative instincts their MCU box office suggested, or whether they were competent executors of someone else's vision.

celebrityMentions.name: Simon Stalenhag
celebrityMentions.context: Swedish artist and author of the 2018 illustrated novel The Electric State. Stalenhag's work is characterized by hauntingly beautiful paintings of retro-futuristic landscapes, blending pastoral Scandinavian settings with decaying technology. His previous work, Tales from the Loop, was adapted into an Amazon series. Fans of his source material have been vocal about their disappointment with the film adaptation, arguing it strips away everything that made the novel special: its melancholy, ambiguity, and visual poetry.

parentalGuidance.mpaaDescriptors: Sci-fi violence/action, language and some thematic material
contentWarnings: Sci-fi action violence throughout, including robot battles, explosions, drone attacks, and characters being thrown or knocked around. No blood or gore.

A child (Christopher) is exploited by a corporation, kept in a comatose state while his consciousness is used to power technology. This is thematically disturbing even though it is not graphically depicted.
Michelle disconnects her brother from the Neurocaster system, resulting in his physical death. This is presented as a mercy killing and is emotionally intense.
Multiple uses of profanity including 'shit,' 'ass,' 'damn,' 'hell,' 'bitch,' 'bastard,' 'dick,' and one near-use of 'motherfucker.' Multiple misuses of God's and Jesus's names.
Brief mocking reference to the Holy Trinity that some viewers may find offensive.
Eight obscene hand gestures throughout the film.
No sexual content. One mild innuendo about an '8 inch model' from a robot character.
Themes of death, grief, loss of family, foster care, and corporate exploitation of children.
Anti-technology messaging: characters who use Neurocaster headsets are depicted as semi-vegetative and disconnected from reality. Parallels to screen addiction are explicit.
Intense robot-on-robot and robot-on-human violence in the climactic battle sequence.
parentalGuidance.guidance: Rated PG-13 for sci-fi violence/action, language, and thematic material. The violence is primarily sci-fi action with no blood or gore, though robot destruction and battle sequences are frequent and intense. Language is moderate, with multiple mild profanities and religious exclamations scattered throughout. The most significant content concern for parents is thematic: a child is kept comatose and exploited by a corporation, and the protagonist ultimately has to let her brother die to free him. These themes of child exploitation, grief, and mercy killing are heavy for younger viewers. The anti-screen/anti-technology message is timely but delivered with a sledgehammer. Suitable for the PG-13 rating. Conservative parents should note the found-family emphasis over biological family, the competent-but-snarky female lead archetype, and the anti-corporate messaging. None of these are extreme, but they are present.

summary.overall:
The Electric State is a $320 million argument that money cannot buy a soul.

The Russo Brothers, riding the lingering fumes of their Avengers: Endgame triumph, took Simon Stalenhag's hauntingly beautiful illustrated novel about a girl and her robot wandering a decaying alternate America and turned it into a bloated, quip-heavy adventure film that has more in common with a theme park ride than the melancholic art book that inspired it. The result is Netflix's most expensive original film ever made, and one of its most critically savaged: 14% on Rotten Tomatoes from 158 reviews, with a 3.7/10 average rating.

The film is set in an alternate 1994 where a war between humans and sentient robots has left the world fractured. Ethan Skate (Stanley Tucci), a tech CEO, developed Neurocaster technology that let humans upload their consciousness into drone robots, helping win the war but creating a society of screen-addicted zombies who live vicariously through their machines. Teenager Michelle Greene (Millie Bobby Brown) lost her family in a car crash years ago and lives with Ted (Jason Alexander), an incompetent foster father who spends his days in a Neurocaster stupor. When a small robot named Cosmo (voiced by Alan Tudyk) appears and convinces Michelle that her genius brother Christopher is still alive, she sets off across the country to find him.

Along the way, she reluctantly teams up with Keats (Chris Pratt), a smuggler and war veteran who exists primarily to deliver wisecracks and provide the audience a familiar Marvel-adjacent presence. Keats has a robot sidekick named Herman (voiced by Anthony Mackie) who transforms between various forms and serves as comic relief. Together, they reach the Exclusion Zone, a robot refugee settlement led by Mr. Peanut (Woody Harrelson voicing a sentient version of the Planters mascot, which is somehow a thing that happens in this film).

The plot eventually reveals that Christopher was found alive after the crash but exploited by Skate's corporation Sentre, his prodigious intellect harvested to power the Neurocaster system. Dr. Amherst (Ke Huy Quan), the scientist who certified Christopher's death, has been hiding in the Exclusion Zone out of guilt. The climax involves Michelle infiltrating Sentre headquarters, discovering her brother trapped in a comatose state, and making the gut-wrenching decision to disconnect him, knowing it will kill his body but free his consciousness.

The final act twist, where Christopher's death shuts down Skate's drone army and Michelle broadcasts a speech inviting the world to unplug and rebuild, is the kind of earnest, on-the-nose messaging that would feel powerful in a better film but lands with a thud here because the two hours preceding it have been so tonally inconsistent. The movie careens between slapstick robot comedy, generic action sequences, and moments of genuine emotional weight without ever finding a rhythm.

Millie Bobby Brown carries the film on sheer screen presence, though critics and audiences are divided on whether her performance is 'determined and emotionally grounded' or 'the same sassy, bossy archetype she plays in everything.' The truth is somewhere in between. Brown does her best work in the quieter scenes with Ke Huy Quan and Woody Norman (as Christopher), but the script never gives her enough vulnerability to make the emotional payoff land. Michelle is always in control, always right, always the smartest person in the room. She tells adults what to do. She outsmarts the villain. She saves the world. The character reads less like a traumatized teenager and more like a focus-grouped composite of what a $320 million film thinks its target audience wants to see.

Chris Pratt is fine. He is doing exactly what Chris Pratt does: charming, goofy, slightly roguish, fundamentally decent. The problem is that his character was invented for the film and feels like it. Keats exists to give the movie a bankable male lead and to provide the buddy-comedy dynamic the Russos clearly felt the source material lacked. Pratt and Brown have adequate chemistry, but the relationship never deepens beyond surface-level banter.

The CGI is simultaneously the film's greatest achievement and its most damning indictment. $320 million is visible on screen: the robots are detailed, the world-building is dense, and the Exclusion Zone sequences have a real sense of scale. But the sheer volume of digital artifice creates a numbing effect. When everything is CGI, nothing feels real. The practical-effects charm that made characters like Grogu or the original Terminator enduro-skeleton memorable is entirely absent. Every robot, every environment, every explosion exists in a digital soup that the eye eventually stops processing as tangible.

The 74% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes tells a different story than the 14% critic score. General audiences, particularly families, found the film entertaining enough. It drew 25.2 million views in its opening week and accumulated 74.2 million views in its first half-year on Netflix. Those are not catastrophic numbers in isolation. But against a $320 million budget, they represent a significant underperformance. Netflix expected this to be their Avengers. Instead, it performed below even The Gray Man, the Russos' previous Netflix misfire.

The culture war discourse around the film has been predictable. Progressive critics have focused on the film's failure as art, its derivative storytelling, and its wasteful budget. Conservative commentators have zeroed in on the 'girl-boss' lead, the found-family-over-blood-family themes, the incompetent foster father played for laughs, and the anti-corporate messaging as evidence of Hollywood's continued ideological drift. The truth, as usual, is more boring than either camp admits: The Electric State is not a culture war weapon. It is a mediocre film that cost too much money, failed to capture the spirit of its source material, and represents the diminishing returns of the Marvel formula when applied outside the MCU's carefully managed ecosystem.

The Russo Brothers' post-Marvel decline is now a three-film trend. Cherry (36% RT), The Gray Man (51% RT), The Electric State (14% RT). The trajectory suggests that their Avengers-era success was less about their directorial vision and more about the machinery of Marvel Studios, Kevin Feige's oversight, and the gravitational pull of beloved IP. Left to their own devices, the Russos make expensive, competent, soulless blockbusters that audiences consume and immediately forget.

The most damning thing about The Electric State is not that it is bad. It is that it is forgettable. $320 million spent to create a film that will be a Netflix thumbnail people scroll past by 2027.
summary.adultInsight: Conservative adults will find mild irritants but no dealbreakers. Michelle is a competent female lead who drives the story, but she is not militantly feminist. The found-family theme is present (Michelle bonds with Keats, the robots, and her makeshift crew) but the film's actual emotional core is about biological family: Michelle's entire quest is to find her blood brother. The anti-corporate villain is a standard Hollywood trope rather than a pointed political statement. The foster father being useless is played for laughs but is not a systemic indictment of traditional family structures. The anti-technology message, ironically delivered through one of the most technology-dependent films ever made, is actually conservative in spirit: put down the screens, go outside, reconnect with real people. Progressive adults will appreciate the female-led adventure and diverse voice cast but will likely be disappointed by the film's superficiality. The anti-tech messaging is not as sophisticated as it thinks it is. The film never interrogates its own position as a streaming spectacle telling audiences to stop streaming. Overall, this is an ideologically mild film that leans slightly progressive through its casting and character dynamics but does not push any aggressive agenda. Its biggest crime is mediocrity, not ideology.
summary.parentalGuidance: Rated PG-13 for sci-fi violence/action, language, and thematic material. Action violence is frequent but bloodless: robot battles, explosions, and drone combat dominate the final act. Language includes multiple uses of 'shit,' 'damn,' 'hell,' 'ass,' 'bitch,' and one near-use of 'motherfucker.' Several misuses of God's name and Jesus's name. No sexual content beyond one mild robot innuendo. The heaviest content is thematic: a child exploited by a corporation, a mercy killing of a sibling, grief and foster care. The anti-screen message is heavy-handed but appropriate for family discussion. Suitable for teens 13 and up. Younger children will enjoy the robot characters but may be disturbed by Christopher's fate.

tropeAudit.name: Girl-Boss Lead / Hyper-Competent Female Protagonist
tropeAudit.description: Michelle Greene is the unquestioned driver of every decision in the film. She rejects foster care, defies her school, initiates the quest, recruits Keats (who she orders around), devises the infiltration plan, and ultimately saves the world by disconnecting the Neurocaster. Male characters exist to assist her or get out of her way. Keats, despite being a war veteran and smuggler, defers to Michelle repeatedly. The film never presents a meaningful challenge that Michelle cannot overcome through sheer determination. This is not the most aggressive version of the trope (Michelle does show genuine emotion about her brother and is not invulnerable), but the pattern is unmistakable. Weighted: 3 x 0.7 x 1.8 = 3.78

tropeAudit.name: Found Family Elevated Over Biological Family
tropeAudit.description: Michelle's biological parents are dead. Her foster father Ted is depicted as an incompetent, screen-addicted deadbeat. The family Michelle builds during her journey, Keats, Herman, Cosmo, the Exclusion Zone robots, becomes her true support system. The film ends with Michelle choosing to live among her found family in the rebuilt Exclusion Zone. However, this trope is partially offset by the fact that Michelle's entire motivation is biological: she crosses the country to find her blood brother. The emotional climax is the biological sibling bond. The found family is the frame, but the biological connection is the beating heart. Score adjusted downward for this counterbalance. Weighted: 2 x 0.7 x 1.0 = 1.4

tropeAudit.name: Incompetent/Absent Father Figure
tropeAudit.description: Ted Finister (Jason Alexander) is Michelle's foster father and is portrayed as a complete failure. He spends his days using a Neurocaster headset instead of parenting, is disconnected from Michelle's life, and operates a drone for lazy personal errands. He is played strictly for comedy: the bumbling, checked-out male guardian that the capable female protagonist must escape. No positive father figure exists anywhere in the film. Dr. Amherst comes closest but functions as a mentor, not a father. The absence of any competent male authority figure is noticeable. Weighted: 3 x 0.7 x 0.5 = 1.05

tropeAudit.name: Anti-Corporate / Eat-the-Rich Villain
tropeAudit.description: Ethan Skate (Stanley Tucci) is the film's primary antagonist: a tech CEO who exploited a child's consciousness to build a world-dominating technology platform, then used his drones to control society while people stayed addicted to his product. He is a thinly veiled composite of every Silicon Valley boogeyman: Jobs's charisma, Zuckerberg's surveillance capitalism, Musk's drone ambitions. The corporate-villain-as-source-of-all-evil is a Hollywood staple that reads as distinctly progressive in its framing: the problem is not human nature but corporate greed, and the solution is dismantling the corporation. The film has no nuance on this point. Skate is purely evil, his company is purely exploitative, and his defeat is purely liberating. Weighted: 3 x 1.0 x 1.8 = 5.4

tropeAudit.name: Anti-Technology / Screen Addiction Messaging
tropeAudit.description: The Neurocaster technology is an explicit metaphor for screen addiction. Users put on headsets and check out of reality, letting drones handle their lives. Michelle is one of the few people who refuses to use the technology, making her exceptional by virtue of being unplugged. The film ends with her broadcasting a message to the world: unplug, go outside, reconnect with real humans. This anti-technology message is not inherently left or right (conservatives and progressives both criticize Big Tech), but the film frames it through a distinctly progressive lens: the technology was created by a corporate villain to control people, and liberation comes through collective action and community, not individual choice or market forces. Weighted: 2 x 1.0 x 1.0 = 2.0

tropeAudit.name: Biological Family Bond as Emotional Core
tropeAudit.description: Despite the found-family framing, the film's actual emotional engine is entirely biological. Michelle's quest is motivated by one thing: finding her blood brother. Every decision she makes, every risk she takes, is driven by the sibling bond. The climax is Michelle choosing to free Christopher even though it means losing him. The post-credits tease (Cosmo reactivating) suggests Christopher's consciousness lives on, preserving the biological connection. The film never suggests that the found family could replace the brother. It supplements but does not substitute. This is the film's strongest traditional element. Weighted: 4 x 0.7 x 1.8 = 5.04

tropeAudit.name: Self-Sacrifice and Personal Responsibility
tropeAudit.description: Michelle makes the ultimate sacrifice: she disconnects her brother, knowing it will kill his body, because she understands it is the right thing to do. This is a genuinely traditional moral framework, accepting painful duty over personal desire. Keats also demonstrates self-sacrifice by risking his life in the assault on Sentre without personal motivation. Dr. Amherst's years of guilt-driven exile and his ultimate death protecting the truth also embody personal responsibility. These moments of individual moral courage are the film's most traditional elements. Weighted: 3 x 0.7 x 1.0 = 2.1

tropeAudit.name: Anti-Screen / Return to Reality Message
tropeAudit.description: The film's conclusion has Michelle urging the world to unplug from Neurocaster technology and reconnect with the physical world. This message aligns with conservative concerns about screen addiction, social media's corrosive effects, and the loss of genuine human connection. The irony that this message is delivered through a $320M streaming film on Netflix is significant, but the message itself resonates with traditional values about embodied community, face-to-face relationships, and the dangers of escapism. Weighted: 2 x 0.7 x 0.5 = 0.7

tropeAudit.name: Military Service Treated With Respect
tropeAudit.description: Keats is a war veteran whose military experience gives him practical skills that prove essential to the mission. Marshall Bradbury (Giancarlo Esposito) is a military figure who ultimately defects from the villain's side out of moral conviction. Military service is not mocked or problematized. Veterans are presented as capable, if flawed, individuals whose combat experience has value. Bradbury's defection is framed as an act of individual conscience, not an indictment of military culture. Weighted: 2 x 0.7 x 0.5 = 0.7

tropeAudit.name: Redemption Through Moral Choice
tropeAudit.description: Multiple characters achieve redemption through deliberate moral choices. Bradbury defects from Skate's army when he witnesses the extent of the corporate evil. Keats transforms from self-interested smuggler to selfless protector. Dr. Amherst spends years in exile atoning for his role in Christopher's exploitation and ultimately dies protecting the truth. The film consistently presents moral agency as a matter of individual choice rather than systemic determinism. People choose to do the right thing when it matters. Weighted: 2 x 0.7 x 0.7 = 0.98
